title: Pakistan Name 20-Member Hockey World Cup Squad as India Pool Clash Awaits
excerpt: The Pakistan Hockey Federation has unveiled its squad for the FIH Men's Hockey World Cup 2026 in the Netherlands and Belgium, with a newly appointed captain leading the side into a tough Pool D alongside India, England, and Wales.
body:
• Pakistan Hockey Federation names 20-member squad for FIH Men's Hockey World Cup 2026, running August 15–30 in the Netherlands and Belgium.
  • Abu Bakar Mahmood replaces veteran Ammad Butt as captain after 14 years, marking a generational leadership shift.
  • Pakistan drawn in Pool D alongside India, England, and Wales — setting up a high-stakes India-Pakistan encounter on hockey's biggest stage.
  • The Green Shirts enter the tournament after losing all 16 matches in the FIH Pro League, raising questions about their competitiveness against top-ranked opposition.

The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) has announced a 20-member squad for the FIH Men's Hockey World Cup 2026, scheduled to be held jointly in Amstelveen, the Netherlands, and Belgium from August 15 to 30. The squad selection comes amid one of the most turbulent periods in Pakistan hockey's storied history.

New Captain, New Era

In a significant leadership change, Abu Bakar Mahmood has been named captain of the national team. The PHF announced the appointment on July 29, replacing Ammad Butt, who had held the captaincy for 14 years. The federation's Professional Development Committee recommended the change, though Butt remains in the squad as a senior player.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XlWihrNWNAI

"Under Abu Bakar's leadership and with the experience of senior players alongside younger members of the squad, the team will continue to develop into a competitive unit."

— Pakistan Hockey Federation statement

The 20-member squad includes goalkeepers Waqar and Ali Raza, alongside Muhammad Abdullah, Muhammad Sufyan Khan, Moeen Shakeel, Abdul Waheed Ashraf Rana, Abdul Hanan Shahid, Zakaria Hayat, Arshad Liaqat, Adeel Latif, Ahmad Nadeem, Ghazanfar Ali, Imad Shakeel Butt, Muhammad Hamaduddin Anjum, Rehman Abdul, Afraz, Umar Mustafa, Abu Bakar Mahmood, Abdul Matan, and Muhammad Imad.

Dutch coach Bob Johan Veldhof leads the technical staff as head coach, with Great Britain's Christopher John Bowen and Pakistan's Adnan Zakir serving as assistant coaches. Muhammad Owais Qarni has been appointed team manager.

Pool D: India, England, and the Rivalry That Matters

Pakistan have been drawn in Pool D alongside England, India, and Wales, setting up what promises to be one of the tournament's most anticipated group-stage clashes. The India-Pakistan hockey rivalry stretches back decades, with both nations having won the World Cup in their respective golden eras — Pakistan four times and India once.

For South Asian hockey fans, and particularly for diaspora communities in North America, the UK, and Europe, the pool-stage encounter carries emotional weight that transcends sport. India and Pakistan haven't met at a Hockey World Cup since 2018, and the matchup in the Netherlands could draw significant global attention.

A Long Road Back

Pakistan enter the tournament under a cloud. The Green Shirts suffered defeats in all 16 of their FIH Pro League matches against the world's top-ranked teams, a run that exposed deep structural problems in the country's hockey programme. The sport, once a source of immense national pride, has struggled with underfunding, administrative dysfunction, and a declining talent pipeline.

Pakistan have won four Hockey World Cups — in 1971, 1978, 1982, and 1994 — but haven't reached a final since. Their qualification for this tournament was itself a milestone given recent struggles, and PHF President Mohyuddin Ahmed Wani has urged fans to rally behind the squad.

What's Next

The Hockey World Cup features 16 teams competing across venues in Amstelveen and Belgium. Pakistan's pool-stage campaign will test whether the new leadership and squad blend can compete against established hockey powers. For the team's young players, it represents a chance to stake their claim on the international stage. For the country's hockey faithful, it's a chance to remember what the sport once meant — and perhaps catch a glimpse of what it could mean again.
